text:
Product
Source
Fields
Domains




Paleoclimate-PMIP3-<model>-<experiment>
PMIP3/CMIP5 (Braconnot et al., 2012, doi:10.1038/nclimate1456): climatologies of the PMIP variability database (CVDP), 8 models, experiments lgm, midHolocene, piControl
t2m_ann, t2m_djf, t2m_jja, sst_ann (degC), pr_ann, pr_djf, pr_jja (mm d-1); z_srf (m), f_land, f_ice of the model and experiment (CMIP5 fixed fields; not f_ice of FGOALS-g2 lgm, z_srf and f_land of MPI-ESM-P lgm)
Antarctica, GreenlandPaleo, Greenland, North, Laurentide, Eurasia, Global


Paleoclimate-PMIP3-<experiment>-mean, Paleoclimate-PMIP3-<experiment>-stdev
Ensemble mean and standard deviation of the 8 PMIP3 models, for each experiment
as the models, with n_<field>, the number of models with a value
as above


Paleoclimate-PMIP3-lgm-boundary-conditions
PMIP3 LGM boundary conditions (Abe-Ouchi et al., 2015, doi:10.5194/gmd-8-3621-2015)
dz_srf (m), f_land, f_ice
as above


Paleoclimate-PMIP4-<model>-<experiment>
PMIP4/CMIP6 (Kageyama et al., 2018, doi:10.5194/gmd-11-1033-2018): climatologies of the last 100 years, 4 models (AWI-ESM-1-1-LR, INM-CM4-8, MIROC-ES2L, MPI-ESM1-2-LR), experiments lgm, midHolocene, piControl
t2m_*, pr_* (annual, DJF, JJA, monthly), z_srf, f_land, f_ice
as above


Paleoclimate-PMIP4-<experiment>-mean, Paleoclimate-PMIP4-<experiment>-stdev
Ensemble mean and standard deviation of the 4 PMIP4 models, for each experiment
as the models, with n_<field>
as above


Paleoclimate-CLIMBER3a-<simulation>, Paleoclimate-CLIMBER3a-<simulation>-ocean
CLIMBER-3α (Montoya and Levermann, 2008, doi:10.1029/2007GL032560): present day (present) and LGM with wind stress x 1.7, weak and strong Atlantic overturning (lgm_1p7weak, lgm_1p7strong); atmosphere at 22.5° x 7.5°, ocean at 3.75°
atmosphere: t2m_ann, t2m_jja (degC), pr_ann (mm d-1), z_srf (m), f_land of the model; ocean: to (potential temperature, degC) on depth, mask_ocn
Antarctica, GreenlandPaleo, Greenland, North, Laurentide, Eurasia, Global


Paleoclimate-CLIMBERX-Willeit2025-<state>, Paleoclimate-CLIMBERX-Willeit2025-<state>-ocean
CLIMBER-X (Willeit et al., 2025, doi:10.1038/s41561-025-01814-0), 5°: climate states of the reference simulation under mid-glacial (MIS3) conditions, interstadial, stadial and heinrich (Heinrich stadial), means of the model years of each state (classified by the Atlantic overturning, see ../Willeit2025_climberx/README.md), and the preindustrial control piControl
t2m_*, sst_* (degC), pr_* (mm d-1), f_sic_*, monthly (_mon) and annual (_ann), with their anomalies relative to piControl (*_anom), z_srf, f_land, f_ice of the model; ocean: to (degC), so (psu) on depth, with to_anom, so_anom, mask_ocn
Antarctica, GreenlandPaleo, Greenland, North, Laurentide, Eurasia, Global


Paleoclimate-CLIMBERX-Willeit2025-<run>-transient, ...-<run>-transient-ocean
The same simulations, HS4 (40-32 ka of the model calendar) and piControl: their 2D output (one model year every 100 years, every 1000 years for piControl), on the model grid
t2m_mon, pr_mon, sst_mon, f_sic_mon on month and time, state of each record; annual series on time_ann (amoc, t2m_glob, t2m_grl, co2, hosing, sic_ext_nh, …); ocean: to, so on depth and time, the Atlantic overturning streamfunction moc_atl
Global (GLOBAL-5DEG only)


Paleoclimate-Buizert2018, Paleoclimate-Buizert2018-1981-2010
Buizert et al. (2018): Greenland monthly temperature and precipitation, 22 ka to present, decadal, doi:10.25921/psvs-yg80; and its 1981-2010 baseline
tas (K), pr (kg m-2 s-1) on month and time (years ago), z_srf
Greenland


Paleoclimate-Badgeley2020
Badgeley et al. (2020): Greenland temperature and precipitation from data assimilation, 20 ka to present, 50-year means, doi:10.18739/A2599Z26M
tas_anom (K), pr_frac, pr_frac_low, pr_frac_high (relative to 1850-2000 CE) on time (years ago)
Greenland



On the mountain-glacier domains (Pyrenees, Patagonia, Himalaya), on their 2 km grid: the ensemble means and standard deviations of PMIP3 and PMIP4 (-mean, -stdev; not the members); their nests and crops get these by cropping (see Nests and crops).
The model output is on the models’ own grids (some Gaussian), remapped conservatively. Products are made on grids of 8 km and coarser (16 km for the Buizert et al. time series, 32 km for CLIMBER-3α and CLIMBER-X, which are also on global grids of 1° and coarser): finer grids add no information to these sources, and models can remap them online. Each file also has f_valid, the fraction of each cell covered by the source. The ensemble products are made from the files of the models on each grid: in each cell, the mean or the standard deviation (population) of the models with a value there (e.g. sst_ann only over the ocean of each model), n_<field> models.

title: Paleoclimate: simulations and reconstructions of past climates
text: The float fields are rounded on output to a tolerance by kind (see Precision and file sizes): temperatures to 0.01 K; precipitation to 1%; z_srf and dz_srf to 0.01 m; fractions (f_*, pr_frac*) to 0.001. The ensemble products are computed from the rounded products of their members and rounded again.

title: RSL: relative sea level indicators
text:
Dated relative sea level indicators (index points and limiting data). RSL is a records dataset (non-gridded data, see Records): its products, defined in RSL/records.toml, are prepared files in the form of the CF discrete sampling geometries, written to $FESMDATA/Records/RSL/RSL-<product>.nc.





Product
Source
Region
Variables




RSL-GAPSLIP
GAPSLIP 2.1 (Gowan, 2023), doi:10.5281/zenodo.10121689
Greenland: 1019 samples at 47 locations, up to 44 ka
rsl, rsl_min, rsl_max (m, 2σ), type (marine limiting, index point, terrestrial limiting), time, time_min, time_max (years ago, 2σ), lab_id, site_name, sector, reference



Each sample is an observation (featureType point, dimension obs) with its lat, lon and time in years before 1950 CE (units “years ago”, calibrated ages).










Source
Licence




GAPSLIP 2.1 (Gowan, 2023)
CC BY-SA 4.0 (repository; the Zenodo record states CC BY 4.0)

title: Sediment: sediment thickness and properties
text:
Sediment thickness (m) from global and regional maps, and sediment properties of North America and Greenland, remapped onto the grids of the domains and onto global lon-lat grids. Sediment is a thematic dataset made by remapping (see Gridded data): its products are defined in Sediment/remap.toml.





Product
Source
Fields
Domains




Sediment-CRUST1
Laske et al. (2013): CRUST1.0, 1° global crustal model, land and ocean (igppweb.ucsd.edu/~gabi/crust1.html); its sediments are those of Laske and Masters (1997), the global sediment map of the v1 product SED-L97, which it replaces
z_sed (total), z_sed_upper, z_sed_middle, z_sed_lower (layers)
Antarctica, GreenlandPaleo, Greenland, North, Laurentide, Eurasia, Global

Each file <GRID>_Sediment-<Source>.nc also has f_valid, the fraction of each cell covered by the source. Each source is remapped conservatively; on grids finer than the source it is then smoothed with a Gaussian of half the source spacing. CRUST1.0 contains the sediment map of Laske and Masters (1997) (A Global Digital Map of Sediment Thickness, EOS Trans. AGU, 78, F483; igppweb.ucsd.edu/~gabi/sediment.html) unchanged: on its 1° grid, the total thickness and the three layers agree with the original files (sedmap.map, map1.thk1-3) to within 0.01 km, the rounding of the stored values. The classes of Gowan et al. (2019) are remapped as classes: each cell gets the class that covers most of it. The global attribute remap_method records what was done on each grid.



The float fields are rounded on output to a tolerance by kind (see Precision and file sizes): the thicknesses (z_sed*) to 0.01 m; f_valid to 0.001. The classes of Gowan2019 are exact.

title: SMBObs: surface mass balance observations
text:
Point measurements of the surface mass balance of the ice sheets. SMBObs is a records dataset (non-gridded data, see Records): its products, defined in SMBObs/records.toml, are prepared files in the form of the CF discrete sampling geometries, written to $FESMDATA/Records/SMBObs/SMBObs-<product>.nc.





Product
Source
Measurements
Variables




SMBObs-SUMup2025
SUMup 2025 (Vandecrux et al., 2025), doi:10.18739/A2M61BR5M
2.74 million in Greenland and Antarctica (cores, pits, stakes, radar, …), 871-2025 CE
smb_total, smb_total_sd (kg m-2, SMB of the measurement interval time_bnds), smb, smb_sd (kg m-2 yr-1, mean rate over the interval), z_srf, keys and tables of the name, method and reference



Each measurement is an observation (featureType point, dimension obs) with its lat, lon and time (days since 1900-01-01, the middle of the interval). SUMup gives the SMB accumulated over the interval (smb_total); smb is smb_total / duration (see SUMup_smb). The density and subsurface temperature data of SUMup are not included.

title: Topo: high-resolution topography
text:
Bed topography, surface elevation, ice thickness and the area fractions of ocean, land and ice on every grid of every active domain, from the base grid (25 m to 2 km) to the coarsest grid, merged from the best available sources: BedMachine and Bedmap3 for the ice sheets, GEBCO 2026 for the ocean and the rest of the land, and the Copernicus DEM and the IceBoost glacier thicknesses for the mountain glaciers. Topo is made by a pipeline of its own; the Products page shows its versions on each domain, the Domains page the domains and grids.


Each domain has default products, from the latest sources, and variants, from earlier versions of the ice-sheet datasets or other sources; both are released. The sources of a product are merged in order of priority, the first over the others:








Product
Sources, by priority

The variants of Antarctica are merged on ANT-500M, but written only on the grids of 1 km and coarser (variants_resolution in products.toml). The files are <GRID>_TOPO-<product>.nc, with the fields:








Field
Units
Contents




z_bed
m
Bed elevation (cell mean)


z_srf
m
Surface elevation (cell mean; 0 over the ocean; in Antarctica including firn air)


H_ice
m
Ice thickness (cell mean)


z_bed_sd
m
Standard deviation of the bed elevation within the cell


f_ocn, f_land, f_grnd, f_flt
1
Area fractions of ice-free ocean, ice-free land, grounded ice and floating ice


mask

Dominant surface type: 0 ocean, 1 ice-free land, 2 grounded ice, 3 floating ice


src_id

Source with the largest weight in the cell (names in flag_meanings)



The global attributes product and sources give the product and its sources, by priority.



The processing has two stages:

Sources → base grid. Each source is remapped once onto the base grid of a domain (e.g. ANT-500M, GRL-PAL-500M, NH-2KM, PAT-250M, SRG-25M), and the sources are then merged in order of priority (e.g. BedMachine over GEBCO).
Base → all other grids. Every coarser grid, and the crops of a domain (e.g. GRL, LIS, EIS, ASE, THW, NPI, SPI), is remapped from the merged base product.

Remapping is conservative: exact for sources on the same projection as the domain (BedMachine, Bedmap3), and from sub-cell sampling for sources on other grids (GEBCO, Copernicus DEM tiles, IceBoost glacier tiles, the Drang Drung data in UTM). The methods are in FesmUtils.jl and are threaded.


Each source is remapped onto the base grid as z_bed, z_srf, H_ice, z_bed_sd (sub-cell standard deviation of the bed), the area fractions f_ocn, f_land, f_grnd, f_flt, and f_valid (fraction of the cell covered by the source). Sources on the domain projection (BedMachine, Bedmap3) are remapped exactly; GEBCO, and projected sources on another projection (the Drang Drung data), are sampled at about half their resolution within each cell.
Land sources (the Copernicus DEMs GLO-90 and GLO-30) give only the elevation of the land, as 1-degree lon-lat tiles. Each tile overlapping the base grid is remapped exactly conservatively onto the base cells it covers: every pixel, a quadrilateral on the projection of the domain, is weighted by its area in each cell. The file has z_land (mean land elevation), f_land (land fraction; elevations at or below 0 m are ocean), f_valid (fraction covered by the tiles) and z_land_sd, the standard deviation of the land elevation within the cell, from the bilinear interpolation of the pixels sampled at most half a pixel apart and at least 4 x 4 times per cell. On cells smaller than about two pixels, the spread of the pixels themselves would show the pixel lattice beating against the grid (stripes in z_bed_sd on the 25-50 m grids); that of the interpolated surface varies smoothly, and tends there to the resolved slope times the cell size over sqrt(12).
Thickness sources (IceBoost) give only glacier ice thickness, as one tile per glacier on its own projection (UTM). Each tile is sampled at about half its resolution within the base cells it covers, and the file has H_ice (cell mean, 0 off the glaciers) and f_ice (glacier area fraction). The pixels touched by a glacier outline count as glacier in the tiles, so the thickness and area of each tile are scaled to the glacier volume and area given with it (the raw pixels give 2% more volume and 3-6% more area). Tiles still overlap along shared ice divides: where their glacier fractions add up to more than 1, the cell is shared, its glacier fraction and thickness divided by that sum, so that the overlap is not counted twice (this matters on grids of 50-250 m, where a boundary is a large part of a cell). The job log compares the glacier area and volume with those of the tiles, before and after.
Only the tiles overlapping the base grid are read (threaded). Their grids and latitude ranges, from the file headers, are kept in an index per RGI region ($FESMDATA_WORK/topo/tiles/iceboost_v2_rgiNN.tsv), which the first IceBoost job builds in about 5 min, and rebuilds when the files of a region change. With the index, IceBoost takes under a minute for PYR and SRG and about 11 min for NH, mostly for sampling the 74,000 tiles that overlap NH-2KM.



Sources are blended in order of increasing priority: a source replaces the fields below it where it fully covers a cell, with a weight rising linearly from 0 at the edge of its coverage to 1 at a taper width inside it, a property of the source (taper_km in sources.jl, recorded in the file attribute taper_km): 20 km, so that the regional datasets meet GEBCO smoothly, and 0 for the Drang Drung data, whose coverage is smaller than that and whose edge lies on land of nearly the same surface, so that they replace exactly the cells they fully cover. The ice fraction of each cell is then grounded or floating as a whole, by flotation of its mean ice thickness and bed (densities in products.toml). Surface elevation is kept as given by the sources (in Antarctica it includes firn air). The file also has mask (dominant surface type: 0 ocean, 1 ice-free land, 2 grounded ice, 3 floating ice) and src_id (source with the largest weight).
A land source sets the land wherever its tiles reach (without taper, since it meets GEBCO at sea level along the coast): its land fraction becomes ice-free land with its elevation as bed and surface, and the rest of the cell ocean, with the GEBCO bed below it (at most sea level). The bed standard deviation combines both parts.
A thickness source adds its glaciers onto the ice-free land of the sources below it (GEBCO or the Copernicus DEM, whose elevation is the ice surface): the glacier fraction, at most the ice-free land fraction, becomes grounded ice, and the bed is lowered by the cell-mean ice thickness. Glaciers on ocean (e.g. retreated termini) are dropped. Cells with glacier ice are always grounded. In the NH product, BedMachine replaces the glaciers within its coverage.



Every coarser grid and every crop is remapped from the merged base product. Fields and fractions are conservative cell means, z_bed_sd combines the sub-cell variance of the base grid with the variance of the base-grid means, mask is the dominant surface type (ice where the ice fraction is at least one half), and src_id the source covering most of the cell.



Grid extents follow the v1 grids in ../maps, so the v1 grids at 4-32 km are reproduced, except GRL-32KM, which has 53 instead of 54 columns so that its extent matches the finer GRL grids, and the EIS grids, which are shifted by 16 km in y and extended so that they lie on the NH grids at all resolutions (crops are cut from them on demand); the 250 m grid of the SRG nest reproduces the v1 SRG-250M grid. The ice-sheet domains are on polar stereographic projections, the mountain-glacier domains on the projection used for glacier modelling in each region (UTM, NZTM2000, and the Albers equal-area projection of High Mountain Asia).




Surface elevation is 0 over the ocean for all sources.
BedMachine Antarctica: the surface includes firn air (firn), and the ice thickness does not. Lake Vostok is grounded ice.
BedMachine Greenland v4 and v5: non-Greenland land (Canadian Arctic) is ice-free land.
Bedmap3: the transiently grounded ice shelf is floating ice.
Bedmap2 (1 km, GeoTIFFs): rock outcrops are ice-free land, and Lake Vostok is grounded ice. Heights are relative to the GL04C geoid (EIGEN-6C4 for BedMachine).
GEBCO is used as ice-free topography and bathymetry. Its sub-ice grid only has ice thickness for the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets (covered by the regional sources), and differs from the main grid by a few metres elsewhere.
IceBoost v2.0 (Maffezzoli et al., doi:10.5281/zenodo.17724512; RGI 7.0 outlines) gives the ice thickness of the glaciers and ice caps outside Greenland in the NH product, and of the glaciers of the mountain-glacier domains (RGI regions 07, 11, 13-15, 17, 18). BedMachine Greenland v6 uses the same dataset for the peripheral glaciers of Greenland.
Copernicus DEM GLO-90 (ESA, doi:10.5270/ESA-c5d3d65; the edited TanDEM-X DEM, acquisitions 2011-2015, heights above the EGM2008 geoid) gives the land surface of the mountain-glacier products; GLO-30 (1” in latitude) that of the 25-50 m nests San Rafael, Monte Sarmiento, Schiaparelli and Drang Drung (GLO-90 as a variant on SRG, SAR and DDG). IceBoost v2.0 takes its surface features from the TanDEM-X EDEM, from the same acquisitions, so the surface and the glacier thickness are consistent. The ocean is 0 m in its tiles, and there are no tiles over the open ocean; land below sea level is taken as ocean.
Drang Drung Glacier (sommers2025_drangdrung, DDG variant Sommers2025): the surface DEM and ice thickness of the ISSM setup of Sommers (2025, “Seasonal variability in ice velocity driven by subglacial hydrology of Drang Drung Glacier, Western Himalayas: Modeling scripts and data”, doi:10.5281/zenodo.17593643, CC BY 4.0), MATLAB files on UTM zone 43N (EPSG:32643; not stated in the record, but the outline lies on the glacier, and the DEM matches GLO-90 to 12 m (s.d.) on ice-free land at 50 m). The surface is the 2 m DEM of LEGOS and OMP (2025), in heights above the WGS84 ellipsoid (21 m above GLO-90 on ice-free land, the EGM2008 geoid height there): it is converted to heights above the EGM2008 geoid at each point (PROJ, with the EGM2008 grid of the PROJ data, egm2008_geoid), and its voids (29% of the grid, mostly on ice-free slopes, 0.06 km² within the model domain) are filled with the GLO-30 surface (bilinear). The ice thickness is that of Millan et al. (2022, doi:10.1038/s41561-021-00885-z), 50 m, for all glaciers in a 25 x 25 km box (0 off the ice; RGI 6.0 outlines). The source is the DEM grid within that box (20.5 x 24 km), with bed = surface - thickness; it covers 77% of DDG, all but its edges (most of them in the south).





The float fields are rounded on output to a tolerance by kind (see Precision and file sizes): z_bed, z_srf, H_ice and z_bed_sd to 0.01 m, the area fractions (f_*) to 0.001. mask and src_id are exact. The coarser grids are remapped from the rounded base grid and rounded again. The sources on the base grid (step 2) are intermediate files and are not rounded.

The environment variables are set per machine in ../shared/machines/<machine>.env.



All commands are run from the FesmData root after sourcing the machine environment. On Levante, every step can be submitted as a job on a full compute node:
sbatch --job-name=<name> Topo/jobs/run_step.sbatch <script> <args...>
Logs go to Topo/logs/.


List the datasets and whether they are present:
julia --project=Topo Topo/scripts/00_sources.jl
GEBCO 2026 (4 GB zipped), Bedmap3 (2.5 GB), IceBoost v2.0 (one zip per RGI region) and the Copernicus DEM GLO-90 and GLO-30 tiles of the active domains that use them (1-degree tiles, a few MB each) are downloaded automatically (Levante login node):
julia --project=Topo Topo/scripts/00_sources.jl --download
julia --project=Topo Topo/scripts/00_sources.jl --download NZ    # the tiles of one domain (also inactive)
The other sources need a manual download into the path printed by the script:

BedMachine Greenland (v4-v6) and BedMachine Antarctica (v2-v4) (NSIDC), including the versions no longer listed by NSIDC, need a free NASA Earthdata login. With the login in ~/.netrc (machine urs.earthdata.nasa.gov login <user> password <password>):
wget --load-cookies ~/.urs_cookies --save-cookies ~/.urs_cookies \
     --keep-session-cookies -P <folder> <uri>
with <uri> from ../datamanifest.toml.




Write the grid description and grid file of every grid of a domain:
julia --project=Topo -t 8 Topo/scripts/01_grids.jl GRL-PAL
The script also reports which grids match the v1 definitions in ../maps.



Remap each source of a domain onto its base grid (one job per source, about a minute each on a Levante node):
sbatch --job-name=src-GRL-PAL-bm Topo/jobs/run_step.sbatch 02_regrid_source.jl GRL-PAL bedmachine_greenland_v6
sbatch --job-name=src-GRL-PAL-gebco Topo/jobs/run_step.sbatch 02_regrid_source.jl GRL-PAL gebco2026
Each writes $FESMDATA_WORK/topo/<BASE>/<BASE>_<source>.nc (see Sources on the base grid).



Merge the sources of the products of a domain:
sbatch --job-name=merge-ANT Topo/jobs/run_step.sbatch 03_merge.jl ANT [PRODUCTS]
PRODUCTS is default (the default products, if omitted), variants, all, or the name of one product; the same holds for steps 4 and 5. This writes $FESMDATA/<folder>/<BASE>/<BASE>_TOPO-<product>.nc (see Merging).



Remap each product from the base grid onto all other grids of the domain, including the crops (GRL from GRL-PAL, LIS and EIS from NH):
sbatch --job-name=grids-all-ANT Topo/jobs/run_step.sbatch 04_grids.jl ANT [PRODUCTS]
This writes $FESMDATA/<folder>/<GRID>/<GRID>_TOPO-<product>.nc (see Coarser grids and crops).



sbatch --job-name=plots-ANT Topo/jobs/run_step.sbatch 05_plots.jl ANT [PRODUCTS]
This writes plots to $FESMDATA_WORK/topo/plots/ (the base product, ice thickness on all grids, the difference with the v1 product at 16 or 32 km, and for a variant the difference with a default product at 4 km, or on the base grid of DDG), with colour ranges from the data (elevations centred on sea level where there is ocean), and prints the ice area and volume on every grid in the job log as a conservation check (see Glacier area and volume for the glaciers).




jobs/submit_domain.sh submits steps 1-5 of a domain as a chain of jobs (step 2 as one job per source), each starting when the previous step succeeded:
Topo/jobs/submit_domain.sh ANT                # all steps
Topo/jobs/submit_domain.sh ANT 3              # from step 3
Topo/jobs/submit_domain.sh ANT 2 variants     # the variants, from step 2
The third argument selects the products (as for steps 3-5), and step 2 then remaps only their sources.



A source (a new topography dataset, or a new version of one):

Add it to ../datamanifest.toml, with its uri, doi and, for a manual download (e.g. NSIDC), skip_download = true; 00_sources.jl then lists and downloads it.
Add a reader to sources.jl and a branch for it in read_source. A topography source returns (grid, z_bed, z_srf, H_ice, mask) on its native grid, with ascending axes: grid a ProjGrid (any projection) or LonLatGrid, heights in m (surface 0 over the ocean), and mask with the classes OCEAN, LAND, GRND, FLT; all fields are missing where the source has no data (the part of a base cell with data is its f_valid). A source on the projection of a domain is remapped exactly; any other is sampled within each base cell. A source that only gives glacier thickness (like IceBoost) is a thickness source (is_thickness_source, GlacierTiles), and a source that only gives the elevation of the land in lon-lat tiles (like the Copernicus DEM) a land source (is_land_source, DEMTiles).
Use it in a product (below) and run the steps from step 2 for the domain (step 2 only for the new source: 02_regrid_source.jl <DOMAIN> <source>).

A product or a variant is an entry in products.toml: its name and its sources in order of priority, highest first, under [<domain>.products] (default products, released and made by default) or [<domain>.variants] (made on request with variants or all):
[ANT.variants]
"BedMachine-v3" = ["bedmachine_antarctica_v3", "gebco2026"]
Then run steps 2-5 for it (submit_domain.sh ANT 2 BedMachine-v3). The lowest-priority source must be a topography source covering the whole domain (GEBCO), and a land source must come before it. Variants are released with the default products.
A domain: define it in ../shared/domains.toml (see Overview and code), add its densities (rho_ice, rho_sw) and products to products.toml, and run all steps (submit_domain.sh <DOMAIN>). For glaciers outside the IceBoost regions already listed in ../datamanifest.toml (iceboost_v2_rgiNN), add the RGI region there.

title: Topo: high-resolution topography
text:
The processing has two stages:

Sources → base grid. Each source is remapped once onto the base grid of a domain (e.g. ANT-500M, GRL-PAL-500M, NH-2KM, PAT-250M, SRG-25M), and the sources are then merged in order of priority (e.g. BedMachine over GEBCO).
Base → all other grids. Every coarser grid, and the crops of a domain (e.g. GRL, LIS, EIS, ASE, THW, NPI, SPI), is remapped from the merged base product.

Remapping is conservative: exact for sources on the same projection as the domain (BedMachine, Bedmap3), and from sub-cell sampling for sources on other grids (GEBCO, Copernicus DEM tiles, IceBoost glacier tiles, the Drang Drung data in UTM). The methods are in FesmUtils.jl and are threaded.


Each source is remapped onto the base grid as z_bed, z_srf, H_ice, z_bed_sd (sub-cell standard deviation of the bed), the area fractions f_ocn, f_land, f_grnd, f_flt, and f_valid (fraction of the cell covered by the source). Sources on the domain projection (BedMachine, Bedmap3) are remapped exactly; GEBCO, and projected sources on another projection (the Drang Drung data), are sampled at about half their resolution within each cell.
Land sources (the Copernicus DEMs GLO-90 and GLO-30) give only the elevation of the land, as 1-degree lon-lat tiles. Each tile overlapping the base grid is remapped exactly conservatively onto the base cells it covers: every pixel, a quadrilateral on the projection of the domain, is weighted by its area in each cell. The file has z_land (mean land elevation), f_land (land fraction; elevations at or below 0 m are ocean), f_valid (fraction covered by the tiles) and z_land_sd, the standard deviation of the land elevation within the cell, from the bilinear interpolation of the pixels sampled at most half a pixel apart and at least 4 x 4 times per cell. On cells smaller than about two pixels, the spread of the pixels themselves would show the pixel lattice beating against the grid (stripes in z_bed_sd on the 25-50 m grids); that of the interpolated surface varies smoothly, and tends there to the resolved slope times the cell size over sqrt(12).
Thickness sources (IceBoost) give only glacier ice thickness, as one tile per glacier on its own projection (UTM). Each tile is sampled at about half its resolution within the base cells it covers, and the file has H_ice (cell mean, 0 off the glaciers) and f_ice (glacier area fraction). The pixels touched by a glacier outline count as glacier in the tiles, so the thickness and area of each tile are scaled to the glacier volume and area given with it (the raw pixels give 2% more volume and 3-6% more area). Tiles still overlap along shared ice divides: where their glacier fractions add up to more than 1, the cell is shared, its glacier fraction and thickness divided by that sum, so that the overlap is not counted twice (this matters on grids of 50-250 m, where a boundary is a large part of a cell). The job log compares the glacier area and volume with those of the tiles, before and after.
Only the tiles overlapping the base grid are read (threaded). Their grids and latitude ranges, from the file headers, are kept in an index per RGI region ($FESMDATA_WORK/topo/tiles/iceboost_v2_rgiNN.tsv), which the first IceBoost job builds in about 5 min, and rebuilds when the files of a region change. With the index, IceBoost takes under a minute for PYR and SRG and about 11 min for NH, mostly for sampling the 74,000 tiles that overlap NH-2KM.



Sources are blended in order of increasing priority: a source replaces the fields below it where it fully covers a cell, with a weight rising linearly from 0 at the edge of its coverage to 1 at a taper width inside it, a property of the source (taper_km in sources.jl, recorded in the file attribute taper_km): 20 km, so that the regional datasets meet GEBCO smoothly, and 0 for the Drang Drung data, whose coverage is smaller than that and whose edge lies on land of nearly the same surface, so that they replace exactly the cells they fully cover. The ice fraction of each cell is then grounded or floating as a whole, by flotation of its mean ice thickness and bed (densities in products.toml). Surface elevation is kept as given by the sources (in Antarctica it includes firn air). The file also has mask (dominant surface type: 0 ocean, 1 ice-free land, 2 grounded ice, 3 floating ice) and src_id (source with the largest weight).
A land source sets the land wherever its tiles reach (without taper, since it meets GEBCO at sea level along the coast): its land fraction becomes ice-free land with its elevation as bed and surface, and the rest of the cell ocean, with the GEBCO bed below it (at most sea level). The bed standard deviation combines both parts.
A thickness source adds its glaciers onto the ice-free land of the sources below it (GEBCO or the Copernicus DEM, whose elevation is the ice surface): the glacier fraction, at most the ice-free land fraction, becomes grounded ice, and the bed is lowered by the cell-mean ice thickness. Glaciers on ocean (e.g. retreated termini) are dropped. Cells with glacier ice are always grounded. In the NH product, BedMachine replaces the glaciers within its coverage.



Every coarser grid and every crop is remapped from the merged base product. Fields and fractions are conservative cell means, z_bed_sd combines the sub-cell variance of the base grid with the variance of the base-grid means, mask is the dominant surface type (ice where the ice fraction is at least one half), and src_id the source covering most of the cell.



Grid extents follow the v1 grids in ../maps, so the v1 grids at 4-32 km are reproduced, except GRL-32KM, which has 53 instead of 54 columns so that its extent matches the finer GRL grids, and the EIS grids, which are shifted by 16 km in y and extended so that they lie on the NH grids at all resolutions (crops are cut from them on demand); the 250 m grid of the SRG nest reproduces the v1 SRG-250M grid. The ice-sheet domains are on polar stereographic projections, the mountain-glacier domains on the projection used for glacier modelling in each region (UTM, NZTM2000, and the Albers equal-area projection of High Mountain Asia).




Surface elevation is 0 over the ocean for all sources.
BedMachine Antarctica: the surface includes firn air (firn), and the ice thickness does not. Lake Vostok is grounded ice.
BedMachine Greenland v4 and v5: non-Greenland land (Canadian Arctic) is ice-free land.
Bedmap3: the transiently grounded ice shelf is floating ice.
Bedmap2 (1 km, GeoTIFFs): rock outcrops are ice-free land, and Lake Vostok is grounded ice. Heights are relative to the GL04C geoid (EIGEN-6C4 for BedMachine).
GEBCO is used as ice-free topography and bathymetry. Its sub-ice grid only has ice thickness for the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets (covered by the regional sources), and differs from the main grid by a few metres elsewhere.
IceBoost v2.0 (Maffezzoli et al., doi:10.5281/zenodo.17724512; RGI 7.0 outlines) gives the ice thickness of the glaciers and ice caps outside Greenland in the NH product, and of the glaciers of the mountain-glacier domains (RGI regions 07, 11, 13-15, 17, 18). BedMachine Greenland v6 uses the same dataset for the peripheral glaciers of Greenland.
Copernicus DEM GLO-90 (ESA, doi:10.5270/ESA-c5d3d65; the edited TanDEM-X DEM, acquisitions 2011-2015, heights above the EGM2008 geoid) gives the land surface of the mountain-glacier products; GLO-30 (1” in latitude) that of the 25-50 m nests San Rafael, Monte Sarmiento, Schiaparelli and Drang Drung (GLO-90 as a variant on SRG, SAR and DDG). IceBoost v2.0 takes its surface features from the TanDEM-X EDEM, from the same acquisitions, so the surface and the glacier thickness are consistent. The ocean is 0 m in its tiles, and there are no tiles over the open ocean; land below sea level is taken as ocean.
Drang Drung Glacier (sommers2025_drangdrung, DDG variant Sommers2025): the surface DEM and ice thickness of the ISSM setup of Sommers (2025, “Seasonal variability in ice velocity driven by subglacial hydrology of Drang Drung Glacier, Western Himalayas: Modeling scripts and data”, doi:10.5281/zenodo.17593643, CC BY 4.0), MATLAB files on UTM zone 43N (EPSG:32643; not stated in the record, but the outline lies on the glacier, and the DEM matches GLO-90 to 12 m (s.d.) on ice-free land at 50 m). The surface is the 2 m DEM of LEGOS and OMP (2025), in heights above the WGS84 ellipsoid (21 m above GLO-90 on ice-free land, the EGM2008 geoid height there): it is converted to heights above the EGM2008 geoid at each point (PROJ, with the EGM2008 grid of the PROJ data, egm2008_geoid), and its voids (29% of the grid, mostly on ice-free slopes, 0.06 km² within the model domain) are filled with the GLO-30 surface (bilinear). The ice thickness is that of Millan et al. (2022, doi:10.1038/s41561-021-00885-z), 50 m, for all glaciers in a 25 x 25 km box (0 off the ice; RGI 6.0 outlines). The source is the DEM grid within that box (20.5 x 24 km), with bed = surface - thickness; it covers 77% of DDG, all but its edges (most of them in the south).

title: Topo: high-resolution topography
text: The float fields are rounded on output to a tolerance by kind (see Precision and file sizes): z_bed, z_srf, H_ice and z_bed_sd to 0.01 m, the area fractions (f_*) to 0.001. mask and src_id are exact. The coarser grids are remapped from the rounded base grid and rounded again. The sources on the base grid (step 2) are intermediate files and are not rounded.

title: Topo: high-resolution topography
text:
The products of each domain are defined in products.toml. The machine environment and the Julia packages are set up as described under Machines and storage.









Location
Contents




$FESMDATA_SOURCES
Original datasets (see ../datamanifest.toml)


$FESMDATA/<Domain>/<GRID>/
Output: grid_<GRID>.txt, <GRID>_grid.nc, <GRID>_TOPO-<product>.nc


$FESMDATA_WORK/topo/
Intermediate files (sources on base grids, IceBoost tile index)


$FESMDATA_SOURCES/copernicus_glo90/, copernicus_glo30/
Copernicus DEM GLO-90 and GLO-30 tiles of the domains that use them



The environment variables are set per machine in ../shared/machines/<machine>.env.



All commands are run from the FesmData root after sourcing the machine environment. On Levante, every step can be submitted as a job on a full compute node:
sbatch --job-name=<name> Topo/jobs/run_step.sbatch <script> <args...>
Logs go to Topo/logs/.


List the datasets and whether they are present:
julia --project=Topo Topo/scripts/00_sources.jl
GEBCO 2026 (4 GB zipped), Bedmap3 (2.5 GB), IceBoost v2.0 (one zip per RGI region) and the Copernicus DEM GLO-90 and GLO-30 tiles of the active domains that use them (1-degree tiles, a few MB each) are downloaded automatically (Levante login node):
julia --project=Topo Topo/scripts/00_sources.jl --download
julia --project=Topo Topo/scripts/00_sources.jl --download NZ    # the tiles of one domain (also inactive)
The other sources need a manual download into the path printed by the script:

BedMachine Greenland (v4-v6) and BedMachine Antarctica (v2-v4) (NSIDC), including the versions no longer listed by NSIDC, need a free NASA Earthdata login. With the login in ~/.netrc (machine urs.earthdata.nasa.gov login <user> password <password>):
wget --load-cookies ~/.urs_cookies --save-cookies ~/.urs_cookies \
     --keep-session-cookies -P <folder> <uri>
with <uri> from ../datamanifest.toml.




Write the grid description and grid file of every grid of a domain:
julia --project=Topo -t 8 Topo/scripts/01_grids.jl GRL-PAL
The script also reports which grids match the v1 definitions in ../maps.



Remap each source of a domain onto its base grid (one job per source, about a minute each on a Levante node):
sbatch --job-name=src-GRL-PAL-bm Topo/jobs/run_step.sbatch 02_regrid_source.jl GRL-PAL bedmachine_greenland_v6
sbatch --job-name=src-GRL-PAL-gebco Topo/jobs/run_step.sbatch 02_regrid_source.jl GRL-PAL gebco2026
Each writes $FESMDATA_WORK/topo/<BASE>/<BASE>_<source>.nc (see Sources on the base grid).



Merge the sources of the products of a domain:
sbatch --job-name=merge-ANT Topo/jobs/run_step.sbatch 03_merge.jl ANT [PRODUCTS]
PRODUCTS is default (the default products, if omitted), variants, all, or the name of one product; the same holds for steps 4 and 5. This writes $FESMDATA/<folder>/<BASE>/<BASE>_TOPO-<product>.nc (see Merging).



Remap each product from the base grid onto all other grids of the domain, including the crops (GRL from GRL-PAL, LIS and EIS from NH):
sbatch --job-name=grids-all-ANT Topo/jobs/run_step.sbatch 04_grids.jl ANT [PRODUCTS]
This writes $FESMDATA/<folder>/<GRID>/<GRID>_TOPO-<product>.nc (see Coarser grids and crops).



sbatch --job-name=plots-ANT Topo/jobs/run_step.sbatch 05_plots.jl ANT [PRODUCTS]
This writes plots to $FESMDATA_WORK/topo/plots/ (the base product, ice thickness on all grids, the difference with the v1 product at 16 or 32 km, and for a variant the difference with a default product at 4 km, or on the base grid of DDG), with colour ranges from the data (elevations centred on sea level where there is ocean), and prints the ice area and volume on every grid in the job log as a conservation check (see Glacier area and volume for the glaciers).




jobs/submit_domain.sh submits steps 1-5 of a domain as a chain of jobs (step 2 as one job per source), each starting when the previous step succeeded:
Topo/jobs/submit_domain.sh ANT                # all steps
Topo/jobs/submit_domain.sh ANT 3              # from step 3
Topo/jobs/submit_domain.sh ANT 2 variants     # the variants, from step 2
The third argument selects the products (as for steps 3-5), and step 2 then remaps only their sources.



A source (a new topography dataset, or a new version of one):

Add it to ../datamanifest.toml, with its uri, doi and, for a manual download (e.g. NSIDC), skip_download = true; 00_sources.jl then lists and downloads it.
Add a reader to sources.jl and a branch for it in read_source. A topography source returns (grid, z_bed, z_srf, H_ice, mask) on its native grid, with ascending axes: grid a ProjGrid (any projection) or LonLatGrid, heights in m (surface 0 over the ocean), and mask with the classes OCEAN, LAND, GRND, FLT; all fields are missing where the source has no data (the part of a base cell with data is its f_valid). A source on the projection of a domain is remapped exactly; any other is sampled within each base cell. A source that only gives glacier thickness (like IceBoost) is a thickness source (is_thickness_source, GlacierTiles), and a source that only gives the elevation of the land in lon-lat tiles (like the Copernicus DEM) a land source (is_land_source, DEMTiles).
Use it in a product (below) and run the steps from step 2 for the domain (step 2 only for the new source: 02_regrid_source.jl <DOMAIN> <source>).

A product or a variant is an entry in products.toml: its name and its sources in order of priority, highest first, under [<domain>.products] (default products, released and made by default) or [<domain>.variants] (made on request with variants or all):
[ANT.variants]
"BedMachine-v3" = ["bedmachine_antarctica_v3", "gebco2026"]
Then run steps 2-5 for it (submit_domain.sh ANT 2 BedMachine-v3). The lowest-priority source must be a topography source covering the whole domain (GEBCO), and a land source must come before it. Variants are released with the default products.
A domain: define it in ../shared/domains.toml (see Overview and code), add its densities (rho_ice, rho_sw) and products to products.toml, and run all steps (submit_domain.sh <DOMAIN>). For glaciers outside the IceBoost regions already listed in ../datamanifest.toml (iceboost_v2_rgiNN), add the RGI region there.

title: Records
text:
The Records datasets hold data that are not on a grid: ice core series, greenhouse gases, global sea level, benthic δ18O stacks, orbital elements and insolation, relative sea level indicators, borehole temperature profiles, GPS uplift rates, point measurements of the surface mass balance, and freshwater fluxes by region. They are made from the original sources, like the gridded datasets, but not remapped: each product is one NetCDF file, or several (e.g. one per ice core), following the CF conventions for discrete sampling geometries (see Records format), with the sites, their coordinates and the data. Each NetCDF file has a text form next to it (.txt), for reading without a NetCDF library. They are not split by domain: a model reads a file and selects its sites.
Records are released on the domain Records, one package per dataset, and go to $FESMDATA/Records/<Dataset>/<Dataset>-<Product>[-<part>].nc and .txt (see Download):
julia fesmdata.jl list Records              # the records datasets

title: Records format
text:
Time series, site and profile data (ice cores, relative sea level, boreholes, GPS, point SMB, freshwater fluxes, …) are made like the gridded datasets, from the original sources with a documented prepare.jl, but they are not remapped: the prepared files are the product (see Records for the released ones). They go to
$FESMDATA/Records/<Dataset>/<Dataset>-<Product>.nc           # a product of one file
$FESMDATA/Records/<Dataset>/<Dataset>-<Product>-<part>.nc    # or of several, one per part
next to the domain folders of the gridded data, e.g. Records/IceCores/IceCores-Kindler2014.nc or Records/RSL/RSL-GAPSLIP.nc. A product has several files when its data do not share their axes, e.g. the records of several ice cores, each on its own time axis. Each NetCDF file comes with its text form, <...>.txt (see below). Records are not split by domain: a model reads the file and selects its sites.
Inputs derived for one model (e.g. a hosing mask on the grid of one ocean model, or a series rescaled for one model) stay in the repositories of those models. Unpublished data are not included. Making a records dataset from prepared files is described under Adding a dataset.


NetCDF following the CF conventions for discrete sampling geometries (CF 1.11, chapter 9), so that every file is read the same way:








Data
featureType
Example




one or more series at fixed sites
timeSeries
ice cores, GPS uplift, freshwater fluxes by region


vertical profiles at sites
profile
borehole temperatures


isolated observations
point
relative sea level indicators, point SMB


series of profiles at sites
timeSeriesProfile
firn density through time




Sites (station dimension): lat, lon (degrees), site_name (string), and z_srf (m) where known; a region instead of a site gets a region variable. Series of a region without a location (a global mean, a composite of several cores, a stack) have the dimension region with region_name (e.g. "global"), and lat, lon missing.
Time: paleo series use time in years ago (positive, before 1950 CE; units "years ago"); modern series a CF time axis (days since ..., mid-interval values with time_bnds).
Depth: depth (m, positive down) for profiles.
Uncertainties as <name>_sd (or <name>_min/<name>_max for ranges).
The units and names of the gridded datasets where they apply (e.g. smb kg m-2 yr-1, temperatures K).
Global attributes as for prepared gridded files: title, references, doi, license, featureType, plus the provenance attributes.




Each NetCDF file of a record has a text form next to it, the same name with .txt, for reading without a NetCDF library (e.g. in Fortran or a spreadsheet):
# Text form of IceCores-Kindler2014.nc (FesmData record, see https://fesmc.github.io/FesmData/records.html)
# title: ...
# references: ...
# license: ...
#
# station (1): label in column names; site_name, lat, lon
#   NGRIP: site_name="NGRIP", lat=75.1, lon=-42.32
#
# columns: name, units, long name
#   time, years ago, time
#   tas, K, near-surface air temperature
#   ...
#
# 5651 rows (one per time) after the line of column names; missing values are NaN
  time    tas    acc ...
    10.0 243.43 ...

Lines starting with #: the global attributes, the sites (or regions) with their variables, and the columns with their units and long names.
One line of column names, then one line per row, columns separated by spaces.
The rows are along the time (or sample, depth) axis of the record, or are the observations of point data. A variable on the sites and the rows is a column per site, <name>_<site> (e.g. d18O_NGRIP), or <name> for a record of one site; a variable on the rows and another axis is a column per index (e.g. time_bnds_1, time_bnds_2).
Numbers as stored in the NetCDF file (times in the units of the header, not decoded), missing values as NaN, strings in double quotes.
Variables on other axes only (e.g. lookup tables) are named in the header but are only in the NetCDF file. Records whose variables have more than two axes, or that are too large for text, have no text form (text = false in records.toml).

The text form is made from the NetCDF file (fesmdata.jl record, again after stamp at a release), so both have the same data and version.

Series of a region without a location (a global mean, a composite of several cores, a stack) have the dimension region with region_name (e.g. "global"), and lat, lon missing.
Time: paleo series use time in years ago (positive, before 1950 CE; units "years ago"); modern series a CF time axis (days since ..., mid-interval values with time_bnds).
Depth: depth (m, positive down) for profiles.
Uncertainties as <name>_sd (or <name>_min/<name>_max for ranges).
The units and names of the gridded datasets where they apply (e.g. smb kg m-2 yr-1, temperatures K).
Global attributes as for prepared gridded files: title, references, doi, license, featureType, plus the provenance attributes.

title: Records format
text:
Each NetCDF file of a record has a text form next to it, the same name with .txt, for reading without a NetCDF library (e.g. in Fortran or a spreadsheet):
# Text form of IceCores-Kindler2014.nc (FesmData record, see https://fesmc.github.io/FesmData/records.html)
# title: ...
# references: ...
# license: ...
#
# station (1): label in column names; site_name, lat, lon
#   NGRIP: site_name="NGRIP", lat=75.1, lon=-42.32
#
# columns: name, units, long name
#   time, years ago, time
#   tas, K, near-surface air temperature
#   ...
#
# 5651 rows (one per time) after the line of column names; missing values are NaN
  time    tas    acc ...
    10.0 243.43 ...

Lines starting with #: the global attributes, the sites (or regions) with their variables, and the columns with their units and long names.
One line of column names, then one line per row, columns separated by spaces.
The rows are along the time (or sample, depth) axis of the record, or are the observations of point data. A variable on the sites and the rows is a column per site, <name>_<site> (e.g. d18O_NGRIP), or <name> for a record of one site; a variable on the rows and another axis is a column per index (e.g. time_bnds_1, time_bnds_2).
Numbers as stored in the NetCDF file (times in the units of the header, not decoded), missing values as NaN, strings in double quotes.
Variables on other axes only (e.g. lookup tables) are named in the header but are only in the NetCDF file. Records whose variables have more than two axes, or that are too large for text, have no text form (text = false in records.toml).

The text form is made from the NetCDF file (fesmdata.jl record, again after stamp at a release), so both have the same data and version.

title: Machines and storage
text:
The datasets are made on Levante (DKRZ), where the original datasets and the products are; Albedo (AWI) holds a copy and can also run the pipelines. Users who only download products need none of this (see Download).


Each machine has an environment file in this folder (levante.env, albedo.env, macbook.env), sourced from the FesmData root before running anything:
source shared/machines/levante.env
It sets:



Variable
Contents




FESMDATA_MACHINE
The name of the machine; the job scripts source shared/machines/$FESMDATA_MACHINE.env again on the compute node


PATH, JULIAUP_CHANNEL
Julia from juliaup, at the version of the pipelines (see below)


FESMDATA, FESMDATA_SOURCES, FESMDATA_PREPARED, FESMDATA_WORK
The storage folders (see below)


FESMDATA_V1
The folder of the v1 products, which Topo step 5 compares with (optional)


SBATCH_ACCOUNT, SBATCH_PARTITION, SBATCH_QOS
The Slurm account, partition and QOS of the jobs


GITLAB_TOKEN, ZENODO_TOKEN, ZENODO_SANDBOX_TOKEN
The tokens for releases, read from files in the home folder (see Access)



Each variable can be set before sourcing, and then keeps its value. A new machine is a new file with the same variables.



The pipelines use Julia 1.13.1, installed with juliaup:
curl -fsSL https://install.julialang.org | sh
juliaup add 1.13.1
The machine environment selects this version (JULIAUP_CHANNEL). Each pipeline has its own environment (Topo/, Regions/, each source folder with a prepare.jl); install its packages once, from the FesmData root after sourcing the machine environment (on Levante on a login node, since compute nodes have no internet access):
julia --project=Topo -e 'using Pkg; Pkg.instantiate()'
julia --project=Regions -e 'using Pkg; Pkg.instantiate()'
fesmdata.jl installs the packages of Remap/, Records/, Figures/ and Publish/ itself when a command needs them.



The products live in $FESMDATA, and what makes them in sibling folders named after it (fesmdata_dir in ../provenance.jl):








Folder
Variable
Contents




$FESMDATA
FESMDATA
Products, as released: <folder>/<GRID>/, Records/<Dataset>/


$FESMDATA-sources
FESMDATA_SOURCES
Original datasets ($datasets_dir of ../../datamanifest.toml)


$FESMDATA-prepared
FESMDATA_PREPARED
Prepared sources (<source>/prepare.jl), input of remapping and of the records datasets


$FESMDATA-work
FESMDATA_WORK
Intermediate files (Topo, Regions, ensemble members of Remap, plots)



A copy of the products (a model’s machine, a mirror) is thus just $FESMDATA, and ln -s $FESMDATA links it under its own name. Each FESMDATA_<KIND> variable, if set, replaces the sibling folder. On a case-insensitive file system (macOS, Windows), a folder fesmdata next to the FesmData checkout is the checkout itself: choose another place.








Machine
FESMDATA
FESMDATA_WORK




Levante
/work/ba1442/fesmdata
/scratch/<u>/$USER/fesmdata-work (deleted 14 days after the last access)


Albedo
$FORCLIMA/fesmdata
/albedo/scratch/user/$USER/fesmdata-work


Mac (macbook.env)
$HOME/data/fesmdata
$HOME/data/fesmdata-work



On the HPC machines the project folder is shared by the group, and the intermediate files are per user on scratch, where they are deleted after a while without access (the pipelines make them again).
The shared folders are writable by the group of the project through default ACLs, which the files created in them inherit whatever the umask. To set them up on a new machine, or to change who may write later (e.g. read-only products):
for d in $FESMDATA $FESMDATA_SOURCES $FESMDATA_PREPARED; do
    chmod -R g+w $d && find $d -type d -exec chmod g+s {} +
    setfacl -R -m g::rwX -d -m g::rwX $d
done
The products folder has a README for those who browse it, $FESMDATA/README.md, a copy of FESMDATA_README.md (copy it again when it changes, and on a new machine):
cp shared/machines/FESMDATA_README.md $FESMDATA/README.md



The pipelines run their steps as Slurm jobs on full compute nodes, with all cores as Julia threads (Topo/jobs/run_step.sbatch, Regions/jobs/run_step.sbatch, Remap/jobs/remap_dataset.sbatch), submitted from the FesmData root after sourcing the machine environment, e.g.
sbatch --job-name=grids-ANT Topo/jobs/run_step.sbatch 01_grids.jl ANT
Logs go to <Pipeline>/logs/.

title: Publish: releases of the processed products
text:
All commands go through fesmdata.jl at the root of FesmData: julia fesmdata.jl help lists them. Finding and downloading (list, fetch) needs only Julia; the release commands install the packages of Publish/ themselves when needed.
The processed products of the v2 pipelines (Topo, Regions, …) are released on the package registry of the GitLab project fesmc/fesmdata-products (Helmholtz Codebase), and listed on the website. A release of a dataset (tag <dataset>-vX.Y.Z, e.g. topo-v2.0.0) covers all its domains, with one package per domain, dataset and grid, e.g. Antarctica_Topo_ANT-32KM version 2.0.0, with the products of that grid new or changed in that release. A file unchanged since an earlier release stays in the package of the release it was first uploaded at (2.0.0), so that a release uploads, and fetch downloads, only what is new. The grid files of each grid (grid description and grid file) are released once, in the dataset Grids (Antarctica_Grids_ANT-32KM), for all datasets on the grid; fetch gets them with the products. Domains are named by their output folder (folder in ../shared/domains.toml, e.g. Antarctica, Greenland, Patagonia; all are listed on the Domains page). Records datasets (non-gridded data, see Records) have no grids: they are released on the domain Records, with one package per dataset, e.g. Records_IceCores, with its files in $FESMDATA/Records/<Dataset>/.
A release can also be archived on Zenodo, in the fesmc community, for a DOI: one Zenodo record per dataset and domain, with a DOI per version.


Every dataset on a domain has a registry file, ../registry/<Domain>/<Dataset>.toml, with the release ([_RELEASE]: version, tag, date, link to the packages), its DOIs if archived on Zenodo ([_ZENODO]), and one entry per file:
["ANT-4KM_TOPO-Bedmap3.nc"]
uri = "https://codebase.helmholtz.cloud/api/v4/projects/22725/packages/generic/Antarctica_Topo_ANT-4KM/2.0.0/ANT-4KM_TOPO-Bedmap3.nc"
checksum = "sha256:<hex>"
size = 123456789
storage_path = "$datasets_dir/Antarctica/ANT-4KM/ANT-4KM_TOPO-Bedmap3.nc"
$datasets_dir stands for $FESMDATA, so the files land in the usual layout, $FESMDATA/<Domain>/<GRID>/. The uri of a file unchanged since an earlier release is that of the package where it was uploaded (e.g. 2.0.0 in the registry of release 2.1.0). A file that changed since an earlier release also has previous_checksums, the checksums of its earlier releases, so that copies of those are updated. The registry files are also DataManifest.jl databases.



Finding and downloading the products (list, fetch, mirror) is described on the Download page.



The datasets, the GitLab project and the Zenodo metadata (creators, licence, community) are set in datasets.toml. The files of a release on each grid are defined by the pipeline of the dataset (topo_release_files in ../Topo/files.jl: all products of the domain, default and variants; regions_release_files in ../Regions/files.jl; the grid files of the grids with products of any dataset for Grids, grids_files in release.jl), and must all be present. A release of a dataset (here GHF, version 2.0.0) is made on Levante, where the files are, from the files as they were made and checked, and needs a GitLab token (see Access below). It takes four steps. The grid files of its grids must be released in Grids, as they are locally (checksums): when grid files are written again (Topo step 1) or a dataset is released on new grids, release Grids first, the same way.
1. Tag the release (from any checkout, after the changes are on main):
git fetch origin
git tag -a ghf-v2.0.0 -m "GHF v2.0.0" origin/main
git push origin ghf-v2.0.0
2. Stamp the files with the tag, from the usual checkout at the tag (no uncommitted changes):
cd ../FesmData && git pull
source shared/machines/levante.env
julia fesmdata.jl stamp GHF
stamp sets fesmdata_version of every file new or changed since the earlier release to the tag, in place (only the global attributes change). The files unchanged since then (the checksum of their entry in the registry, which must therefore be committed) keep the version they were released at, and are not uploaded or downloaded again. fesmdata_commit stays the commit that made the file, and history records the stamp and the version the file was made at, so that files made before the tag (whose code may differ in details from the tag) can be recognised. The files are not made again: a product is made and checked once, and released as it is. To make a release fully reproducible from its tag instead, make the files again in a clean checkout of the tag (e.g. git worktree add ../FesmData-ghf-v2.0.0 ghf-v2.0.0, then the pipeline there with --overwrite); they then have the tag already.
3. Upload:
julia fesmdata.jl release GHF --dry-run
julia fesmdata.jl release GHF
The release is that of the newest tag of the dataset. The dry run checks every domain (all files present, the new and changed files at the release tag, the unchanged ones at an earlier tag) and lists the files to upload by package. release then uploads the new and changed files of each grid to its package, checks them (sha256), and writes the registry file of each domain, with the entries of the unchanged files kept. A domain without new or changed files gets only its registry, at the version of the release. Requests that fail because the server is busy are tried again after a wait. If it still stops, run it again: files already uploaded are kept, and domains already released are skipped.
4. Commit and push the registry, which also updates the website:
git add registry && git commit -m "registry: GHF v2.0.0" && git push
5. Clean up the files the release replaced, once the release is out (and mirrored, fesmdata.jl mirror, on the other machines): products no longer made (e.g. copies on a crop that now gets them by cropping, grids dropped by the resolution rule) stay in $FESMDATA until pruned, and the files of earlier releases that were replaced stay on the packages page until deleted:
julia fesmdata.jl prune               # or: prune <Dataset> [<Domain>]
julia fesmdata.jl delete GHF          # files of the packages no release refers to
prune lists the files that no record of the registry refers to, by domain and dataset with their size, and deletes them after one confirmation (--yes: none), writing their list to $FESMDATA_WORK/prune-<date>.txt. It keeps the products by cropping (files with a cropped_from attribute, made by fetch and mirror), the products not released (release = false in <Dataset>/remap.toml, e.g. SolidEarth Pan2022), the grid files of grids still in use, and the records (Records/). Run it on every machine with a copy (Levante, Albedo), after mirror there.
delete <Dataset> lists the files of the packages of the dataset, all versions, that no entry of the registry refers to, and deletes them after one confirmation, with the packages left without files. It reads the registry of the checkout, so it only cleans the packages of versions up to the registered release of each domain: those of a later version (an upload not finished, or a release not yet pulled) and of domains without a registry are kept, and can be deleted by version.
At any point, status shows each domain: its local files and their version, its packages on GitLab, and its registered release (and DOI):
julia fesmdata.jl status Topo
All commands take domains after the dataset to work on some only (e.g. upload Topo Antarctica). --allow-untagged skips the release checks, e.g. for a test. delete Topo <version> removes the packages of a version (e.g. of a test, or of a domain no longer released), after one confirmation; packages with files of the registry are not deleted.
To test, use --sandbox: the packages are named test_<Domain>_<Dataset>_<GRID> and the registry files go to registry/_sandbox/, which is not tracked (fetch.jl --sandbox downloads from them). Delete the test packages afterwards:
julia fesmdata.jl release Topo Eurasia --sandbox --allow-untagged
julia fesmdata.jl delete Topo <version> Eurasia --sandbox



A release on GitLab (with its registry) can be archived on Zenodo for a DOI, with the same local files, after step 3:
julia fesmdata.jl archive upload Topo
julia fesmdata.jl archive publish Topo
git add registry && git commit -m "registry: Topo v2.0.1 on Zenodo" && git push
archive upload puts the files of each domain into a draft of the next version of its Zenodo record (a new record the first time); running it again continues the drafts. archive publish checks the drafts, lists them, publishes them after one confirmation (publishing cannot be undone), and adds their DOIs to the registry. Drafts published on the Zenodo website instead are added with archive register Topo. archive status Topo shows the drafts and archived versions; archive discard Topo deletes the unpublished drafts of a dataset, archive drafts lists all unpublished drafts of your account, and archive discard <id> ... deletes drafts by id. The drafts are recorded in registry/_drafts/ (not tracked). With --sandbox, the Zenodo sandbox archives the test releases (registry/_sandbox/).



GitLab (Helmholtz Codebase): uploads need a token of the project: on fesmdata-products, Settings > Access tokens > Add new token, with the role Developer and the scope api (or a personal token with the scope api, for a member of the project). SSH keys do not work for the package registry. Downloads need no token. Store the token in ~/.gitlab_token on the machine with the files (read without being shown or kept in the shell history):
read -s -p "GitLab token: " t && printf '%s' "$t" > ~/.gitlab_token && chmod 600 ~/.gitlab_token && unset t && echo
Zenodo (only to archive): a personal token, on Zenodo, Account > Applications > Personal access tokens > New token, with the scopes deposit:write and deposit:actions, stored the same way in ~/.zenodo_token (and the sandbox one in ~/.zenodo_sandbox_token). A new version of a Zenodo record can only be made by its owner, or by those the owner gives access (the record > Share > “Can manage”).
The machine environments (../shared/machines/*.env) set GITLAB_TOKEN, ZENODO_TOKEN and ZENODO_SANDBOX_TOKEN from these files; a new machine needs the same lines as there. Check with:
source shared/machines/levante.env && [ -n "$GITLAB_TOKEN" ] && echo "token set"



The website and its generated pages are described under Website and figures.

All commands take domains after the dataset to work on some only (e.g. upload Topo Antarctica). --allow-untagged skips the release checks, e.g. for a test. delete Topo <version> removes the packages of a version (e.g. of a test, or of a domain no longer released), after one confirmation; packages with files of the registry are not deleted.
To test, use --sandbox: the packages are named test_<Domain>_<Dataset>_<GRID> and the registry files go to registry/_sandbox/, which is not tracked (fetch.jl --sandbox downloads from them). Delete the test packages afterwards:
julia fesmdata.jl release Topo Eurasia --sandbox --allow-untagged
julia fesmdata.jl delete Topo <version> Eurasia --sandbox

title: Publish: releases of the processed products
text:
A release on GitLab (with its registry) can be archived on Zenodo for a DOI, with the same local files, after step 3:
julia fesmdata.jl archive upload Topo
julia fesmdata.jl archive publish Topo
git add registry && git commit -m "registry: Topo v2.0.1 on Zenodo" && git push
archive upload puts the files of each domain into a draft of the next version of its Zenodo record (a new record the first time); running it again continues the drafts. archive publish checks the drafts, lists them, publishes them after one confirmation (publishing cannot be undone), and adds their DOIs to the registry. Drafts published on the Zenodo website instead are added with archive register Topo. archive status Topo shows the drafts and archived versions; archive discard Topo deletes the unpublished drafts of a dataset, archive drafts lists all unpublished drafts of your account, and archive discard <id> ... deletes drafts by id. The drafts are recorded in registry/_drafts/ (not tracked). With --sandbox, the Zenodo sandbox archives the test releases (registry/_sandbox/).

title: Publish: releases of the processed products
text:
GitLab (Helmholtz Codebase): uploads need a token of the project: on fesmdata-products, Settings > Access tokens > Add new token, with the role Developer and the scope api (or a personal token with the scope api, for a member of the project). SSH keys do not work for the package registry. Downloads need no token. Store the token in ~/.gitlab_token on the machine with the files (read without being shown or kept in the shell history):
read -s -p "GitLab token: " t && printf '%s' "$t" > ~/.gitlab_token && chmod 600 ~/.gitlab_token && unset t && echo
Zenodo (only to archive): a personal token, on Zenodo, Account > Applications > Personal access tokens > New token, with the scopes deposit:write and deposit:actions, stored the same way in ~/.zenodo_token (and the sandbox one in ~/.zenodo_sandbox_token). A new version of a Zenodo record can only be made by its owner, or by those the owner gives access (the record > Share > “Can manage”).
The machine environments (../shared/machines/*.env) set GITLAB_TOKEN, ZENODO_TOKEN and ZENODO_SANDBOX_TOKEN from these files; a new machine needs the same lines as there. Check with:
source shared/machines/levante.env && [ -n "$GITLAB_TOKEN" ] && echo "token set"
